title: Sentinel-controlled loops
goal: Process a stream of unknown length and distinguish a sentinel, end of input and an error.

prerequisites.text: Understand a validated read status and an accumulator.
Explain how a counted loop terminates.

terms.title: Sentinel
terms.definition: A reserved value that controls processing and does not belong to the data.

terms.title: Loop progress
terms.definition: A change bringing the loop closer to termination. Here an iteration reads one record or terminates processing.

terms.title: break
terms.definition: Exits the nearest loop. The remaining statements in its body are skipped.

sections.title: Why it matters
paragraphs: An event log may end at a sentinel −1 or simply run out of input. Both endings are valid. An invalid record is an error and should not masquerade as an empty log.
With while (1), exits are checked in the body just after a read. Mark three exits in a trace: end of input, sentinel and error. The task also limits the number of accepted events.
Choose a sentinel outside the data range. It still has to parse as a value, but it must not be counted.
The stream can end at a command or at EOF. Both allow a report over accepted values. A broken record takes the separate error branch.

sections.title: A short event log
paragraphs: With 5, 7, −1 and 9 on separate lines, trace how many events the program actually accepts. Input after the sentinel is ignored.
Remove the sentinel and the following record. With 5 and 7 the result is the same, but the reason for stopping changes.
steps: Read the next line and check the status first.
Check the reserved −1 before incrementing the event count.
Check the limit of 5 before accepting another event.
Print the accumulated event count after break.

sections.title: A stop signal does not count as data
paragraphs: Incrementing count before checking the sentinel counts the sentinel as a false event. A log starting with the sentinel would incorrectly report one event.
Do not use event after READ_BAD or READ_END. Exiting before reading it keeps the calculation safe. The compiler rejects while () without a condition.

sections.title: Check order for a new sentinel
paragraphs: For temperatures, 999 means stop and 60 is a valid reading. On READ_OK, check for 999 before applying the measurement range.
The contract allows eight readings. After the eighth temperature, a sentinel or EOF is allowed. A ninth temperature is an error.

reading.author: ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14
reading.title: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 — Programming languages — C
reading.purpose: Review the while loop and the effect of break.

selfcheck.prompt: What does the example print for 5, 7, −1 and 9?
feedback: The sentinel and later lines are excluded.

selfcheck.prompt: Which status means there is no new record?
feedback: This is a line or stream error.
End of input is valid without a sentinel.
A value is ready for further checks.

selfcheck.prompt: How can an empty stream and a stream with one blank line be distinguished?
selfcheck.feedback: An empty stream returns READ_END. A blank line has a record boundary but no number and leads to READ_BAD.

practice.title: Summarise temperatures until the sentinel
practice.task: Read one record per line. A temperature is from −40 to 60. 999 ends the summary, and EOF is allowed. Accept up to eight measurements. Print invalid for an error, empty for no measurements, or the count and sum separated by a space. Ignore input after 999.
practice.hint: Check for 999 after READ_OK, before checking the measurement limit or maximum count.
criteria: The sentinel does not affect count and sum.
A blank line and a ninth measurement are rejected.

steps.action: Compare a stream ending with 999 and one ending at EOF.
steps.why: Both reasons for stopping are valid.
steps.expected: Equal measurements produce the same summary.

steps.action: Insert break for 999 in the right place.
steps.why: The sentinel is outside the measurement range.
steps.expected: The sentinel is excluded from calculation.
Eight plus a sentinel work. A ninth temperature is rejected.

exercises.title: Explain the last repetition
exercises.task: Put 999 on the first line and a valid temperature on the second. Trace why processing ends and which value reaches the sum.
criteria: No value contributes to the sum. The output is empty.

teaching.scene: An event log uses a special number to end its report. Count events before that command and confirm that a later record can no longer change the result.

predict.prompt: The sample records are 5, 7, −1 and 9. When does count change, and at which record does the loop stop processing?
predict.answer: 5 raises count to 1 and 7 raises it to 2. −1 stops the loop before another increment. The line with 9 is left unread and the output is 2.

apply.prompt: A log contains 4, 9, 6 and −1. How does the report change from 4, 9 and −1 when one event appears before the marker?
apply.answer: The marker ends both streams. Three events precede it in the first and two in the second. Verify outputs 3 and 2 respectively.

practice.strategy: Write out the cases in order: end of input, invalid input, marker, then an ordinary temperature. Update count and sum together for each accepted value. Test the marker at the start and after two readings.
practice.diagnosis: If `999` produces invalid after two valid readings, inspect whether the marker is recognized before the upper limit on ordinary temperatures.

syntax.explanation: A sentinel commands termination. The break check comes before the counter update, so the marker itself contributes no event.
syntax.mistake: Checking the ordinary range first can reject a valid stop command. Classify the marker separately.
